Writing recommendation letters is an important part of my job, so you're not asking for a favor. If you found this page on your own, email me first and we'll talk about whether I'm the right person to write for you.

## What I Look For

I'll only agree to write a letter if I can write a strong one. A lukewarm letter hurts an application more than it helps, so a no from me isn't a judgment of you: it means someone who knows you better will write you a better letter.

Good grades alone aren't enough. Your grades are already on your transcript, and a letter that only repeats them tells the committee nothing new. I need to be able to say something about you that the transcript can't, such as:

- **Class participation:** asking questions, answering them, and joining discussions.
- **Curiosity:** conversations outside of class about the material, or about mathematics beyond the syllabus.
- **Office hours:** coming regularly, with questions you had already thought about.
- **Improvement:** how you grew over the course, especially after a rough start or a bad exam.
- **Persistence:** staying with a hard problem, and how you responded to feedback.
- **Creative projects:** a course project that went past the requirements or was your own idea.
- **Research and applications:** research experience, with me or with someone else, if I know enough about it to describe your part. I most like to write about work that applies the mathematics from my courses to another field, in a project, an internship or your own research.
- **TA or grader roles:** working for one of my courses, or tutoring and mentoring elsewhere.
- **Helping other students:** explaining ideas to classmates, and being a good teammate on group projects.
- **Communication:** clear writing and clear presentations.
- **Independence:** reading on your own, a reading course, or learning something you needed without being told to.

You don't need all of these. Two or three that I can describe with specific examples make a strong letter. It also helps if I've known you for more than one course, or if we've kept in touch since.

## What to Send Me

Send **one email**, at least **a month before your first deadline**, with the subject line "Recommendation letter: *your name*". Include:

- [ ] CV
- [ ] Unofficial transcript
- [ ] (Draft) statement of purpose
- [ ] Any other work related to the program or to my courses
- [ ] **What you'd like me to highlight** (see below)
- [ ] **PhD applicants only:** a Google Sheet or Excel file listing each program, its deadline, how it collects letters, and a column for me to check off.

**What to highlight.** Don't be modest. **Advocate for yourself**; I'd rather you claim too much than too little. If I don't agree with something, I'll leave it out, but if you don't mention something important, it might not make it into the letter.

## Reminders

If I haven't submitted your letter a week before a deadline, email me a reminder with the subject line "Recommendation letter reminder: *your name*, due *date*". Reminders are welcome, not a bother. They help me make sure nothing slips.

Good luck with your applications!
